planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; the Gleam series descends from the original 1935 AAS-winning 'Golden Gleam' and combines the long flowering stems and fragrance of the old climbing types with a shorter, semi-trailing habit that needs no support.

directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly where plants are to grow, in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; rich soil produces excess foliage at the expense of bloom. The Gleam Hybrids are a semi-trailing strain, spilling gently over container edges or low walls while staying more restrained than fully vining nasturtiums, and unlike many modern compact series they retain some of the sweet fragrance bred out of most newer nasturtiums. Flowers open in a warm mix of gold, orange, salmon, and scarlet above blue-green rounded leaves through the growing season. All parts are edible with the classic peppery, watercress-like bite; use young leaves and buds sparingly and flowers as a garnish or tossed whole into salads.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; soak seed overnight to speed germination. Strawberries and Cream is a semi-trailing nasturtium best displayed where its unusual pale coloring can be seen up close, such as a raised bed edge or hanging container.

directions: Plant in full sun in average to poor, well-drained soil; like other nasturtiums, overly rich ground produces lush leaves but few flowers. Strawberries and Cream is distinguished by soft creamy-yellow petals brushed and speckled with raspberry-red and rose flecks radiating from the throat, a subtler and more painterly color pattern than the solid golds and reds of standard nasturtium mixes. The rounded, umbrella-like leaves and semi-trailing stems make it equally at home cascading from a container or filling a garden edge. Harvest flowers and young leaves for their peppery, watercress-like flavor in salads and as edible garnishes, and let a few seed pods mature if you want to save seed or pickle them as a caper substitute.
sources: Renee's Garden Seeds — Strawberries and Cream Nasturtium

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Vesuvius pairs unusually dark, smoky-bronze foliage with soft salmon-apricot flowers, so give it a spot where the foliage contrast reads as clearly as the bloom.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil; excess fertility encourages foliage over flowers in all nasturtiums. Vesuvius is a compact, semi-trailing British bedding cultivar valued for the combination of muted salmon-pink to apricot flowers held against dusky bronze-green, almost gray-toned leaves — a smokier, more subdued color palette than the bright orange-and-green of typical nasturtium mixes, which makes it a favorite for pastel and dusky-toned edible flower borders. Flowers, leaves, and unripe seed pods are all edible with the characteristic peppery bite; use the flowers whole as a garnish and chop young leaves sparingly into salads or soft cheeses. Deadhead lightly to keep plants tidy, though nasturtiums generally flower continuously without it.
sources: Thompson & Morgan — Tropaeolum majus 'Vesuvius'

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; Pink Surprise flowers most heavily in cool weather and tends to fade or stop blooming once summer heat sets in, so succession sowing extends the harvest.

directions: Sow directly in average, well-drained soil in full sun; calendula tolerates poor soil but blooms best with regular moisture. Pink Surprise produces semi-double to double flowers in soft apricot and cream tones that blush deeper rose-pink toward the petal tips as they age, a departure from the solid gold and orange shades of most pot marigolds. Deadhead spent flowers every few days to prolong bloom and prevent the plant from putting energy into seed production; the edible petals have a tangy, slightly bitter, saffron-like flavor good for scattering over salads, rice, or soups, while whole flower heads can be dried for tea or infused into oil. Plants often self-sow, though seedlings may revert toward plainer orange coloring over generations.
sources: Renee's Garden Seeds — Pink Surprise Calendula

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in fall in mild-winter climates for winter-into-spring bloom; Sunset Buff is an old heirloom strain that performs best in the cool conditions of spring and fall and declines in summer heat.

directions: Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil; overly rich soil produces lanky growth and fewer flowers. Sunset Buff is a heritage strain grown for its unusual muted apricot-buff to dusty-pink double flowers, a soft, antique color quite different from the assertive golds and oranges typical of pot marigold, and it combines well with other pastel-flowered herbs and vegetables in a cutting or kitchen garden. Harvest flowers as they fully open, in the morning after dew has dried, and pull the petals for salads, rice dishes, or infused oil, or dry whole heads for winter tea; regular picking encourages continued flowering over many weeks. Allow a few late flowers to go to seed if you want to save your own for next season, as named heirloom strains can be lost if only hybrid seed is replanted.
sources: Select Seeds — Calendula officinalis 'Sunset Buff'

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early for an earlier bloom flush; Kablouna's tall, sturdy stems and large flower heads make it well suited to cutting-garden rows as well as mixed borders.

directions: Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, watering regularly during bloom for the largest flower heads. Kablouna is an anemone-flowered calendula series in which a raised, crested central cushion of short quilled florets is surrounded by a single or double outer ring of longer petals, giving flowers a distinctly novelty, chrysanthemum-like form in shades of cream, lemon, gold, and orange. The unusual double-tiered flowers hold up especially well as cut flowers and dry easily for winter arrangements or tea. The petals are edible with calendula's characteristic tangy, resinous, saffron-like flavor and can be scattered fresh over savory dishes or dried for later use; deadhead regularly to keep plants blooming from spring into early summer before heat shuts them down.
sources: Swallowtail Garden Seeds — Kablouna Calendula

planting.note: Start indoors 6-10 weeks before last frost, or sow in mid to late summer for fall and winter blooms in mild climates; Etain performs best through the cool months and often slows or pauses in summer heat, resuming again as temperatures cool in fall.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade in hot climates; Etain is a long-blooming English viola holding an RHS Award of Garden Merit, bearing pale primrose-yellow flowers finely edged in soft lavender-violet with a small central yellow eye, a delicate bicolor combination that reads as much subtler than typical bright pansy mixes. It forms a low, spreading mound and flowers over an exceptionally long season when deadheaded regularly and kept from drying out. Like other violas the flowers are edible, with a mild, faintly sweet, wintergreen-like flavor good for garnishing desserts, salads, and drinks; the plant also tolerates light frost and can overwinter in milder zones to bloom again the following spring.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-12 weeks before last frost, or sow in late summer for fall planting and spring bloom in mild-winter climates; Antique Shades flowers best in cool weather and benefits from light afternoon shade once temperatures climb.

directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, in full sun where summers stay cool or partial shade elsewhere. Antique Shades is a Thompson & Morgan pansy series bred for an unusual palette of muted, dusty pastels — soft rose, mauve, cream, apricot, and bronze tones often blending on a single flower — quite different from the saturated primary colors of most bedding pansies, and it has become a favorite for cottage-style and heirloom-themed plantings. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep new flowers coming and prevent the plant from going to seed prematurely. The flowers are edible, with a mild, slightly grassy-sweet flavor, and are popular for decorating cakes, salads, and iced drinks; plants tolerate light frost and often rebloom in fall after a summer rest in warmer climates.
sources: Thompson & Morgan — Viola x wittrockiana 'Antique Shades'
